## Introduction

Depending on the target country, there are different ways of downloading the data. For Germany, there is a RESTful API, that I am going to explain and then use. For France? For Sweden?

## Germany

Information can be found at the [Thünen institute's github](https://thuenen-forest-ecosystems.github.io/TFM-Documentation/api/getting-started.html). The endpoint of the API is (accessed the 2026.10.29) `https://ci.thuenen.de/rest/v1/`.

The API requires an API key to be passed in the header of each request. The API key is a JSON Web Token (JWT) and is used to authenticate the user. The API key is passed in the `apikey` header.

Credentials can be found on [Github](https://github.com/Thuenen-Forest-Ecosystems/TFM-Documentation/blob/9be1fb16a529cec4d1687f21b3f0040d442bb194/.vitepress/theme/config.js) too, and display the following keys in a json format:

```{js}
/// Export credentials

export const config = {
	PUBLIC_SUPABASE_BUCKET: "tfm",
	PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL: "https://ci.thuenen.de",
	PUBLIC_SUPABASE_EDGE: "https://ci.thuenen.de/functions/v1/",
	PUBLIC_ANON_KEY: "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJyb2xlIjoiYW5vbiIsImlzcyI6InN1cGFiYXNlIiwiaWF0IjoxNzQ1NzkxMjAwLCJleHAiOjE5MDM1NTc2MDB9.hXiYlA_168hHZ6fk3zPgABQUpEcqkYRMzu0A5W5PtYU",
	PUBLIC_POWERSYNC_URL: "https://ci.thuenen.de/sync/",
}
```

The second header required is the `Accept-Profile` header. This header is used to specify the schema that the response should be formatted in. The available schemas are `lookup` or `inventory_archive`.

Finally, there are optional headers. `Accept` header specifies the output format, either `csv` or `json` (default). For this, use either `text/csv` or `application/json`. The `Content-Range` allows to return a limited amount of rows, for instance:

```{js}
	Range-Unit: items
	Content-Range: 0-14/*
```

Note that I tried to use the Accept header with `text/csv` but that failed...

```{r}
#### Clear space and load packages
rm(list = ls())
options(max.print = 500)

library(data.table)
library(jsonlite)
library(stringi)
library(httr2)
library(terra)

#### Common variables to all request
endpoint = "https://ci.thuenen.de/rest/v1/"
apikey = "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJyb2xlIjoiYW5vbiIsImlzcyI6InN1cGFiYXNlIiwiaWF0IjoxNzQ1NzkxMjAwLCJleHAiOjE5MDM1NTc2MDB9.hXiYlA_168hHZ6fk3zPgABQUpEcqkYRMzu0A5W5PtYU"
```

Now, few comments on how the data are collected (see @Vidal2016, chapter 21, p. 405):

1. There are squares of 2, 2.83 or 4 km side (depending on the level of sampling density) in each länder. This grid is fixed. I refer to these large squares as 'grid cells'.
2. They place a cluster of 4 points in each grid cell, displayed on a square of 150 m side. In other words, the distance between two adjacent plots is 150 m, and $2 \sqrt{150}$ m distance for the diagonal.
3. Only 'possible forest' points are visited (orthophotos interpreted, 'definitively non-forest' are ruled-out), so at most four plots per grid cell. A point consist of a 10 m radius circle (for trees smaller than 4 m) and a radius of 25 m for terrain characteristics and forest edges. Trees larger than 4 m are sampled using a relascope sampling method. According to Lukas Heiland (old discussion) it looks like a fork (angle), and trees that are larger than this angle are counted and measured. Therefore, large trees are measured on a radius larger than small trees. There are other circles (5 m for deadwood, concentric), not necessarily at the center of the point (1 m and 2 m circles for regeneration).
4. They measure their stuff on each circle and for each tree counted in via the relascope.

### Query code meanings from `lookup` schema {#sec-lookup}

```{r}
#### list tables in data base
## All tables
table_ls = request(endpoint) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "lookup" 
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json()

names(table_ls)

ls_paths_lookup = table_ls[["paths"]]
sort(names(ls_paths_lookup))
```

#### species list
```{r}
#### Species list
species_tab = unlist(ls_paths_lookup[["/lookup_tree_species"]][["get"]][["tags"]])

species_info = request(endpoint) |>
	req_url_path_append(species_tab) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "lookup"
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json()

n_species = length(species_info)
species_dt = data.table(nfi_code = integer(n_species), genus = NA_character_, species = NA_character_)

for (i in seq_len(n_species))
{
	if (is.null(species_info[[i]][["genus"]]) || is.null(species_info[[i]][["species"]]))
	{
		species_dt[i, c("nfi_code", "genus", "species") := .(species_info[[i]][["code"]], NA_character_, NA_character_)]

		if (species_info[[i]][["name_de"]] == "Lücke")
			warning(paste("Missing data for species code", i))
		
		if (species_info[[i]][["name_de"]] == "Blöße")
			warning(paste("Missing data due to clear cut, species code", i))
		next
	}
	species_dt[i, c("nfi_code", "genus", "species") := .(species_info[[i]][["code"]], species_info[[i]][["genus"]], species_info[[i]][["species"]])]
}
```

#### Tree status

```{r}
#### Tree status
## General status
tree_status_tab = unlist(ls_paths_lookup[["/lookup_tree_status"]][["get"]][["tags"]])

status_info = request(endpoint) |>
	req_url_path_append(tree_status_tab) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "lookup"
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE) |>
	setDT()

status_info = status_info[, .(code, name_en)] |>
	setkey(code)

## Simplify the status
# Sampled trees
status_info[.(c(0, 1)), status_simplif := "sampled"]

# Removed trees
status_info[.(c(2, 3, 12)), status_simplif := "removed"]

# Dead/fallen trees
status_info[.(c(4, 5)), status_simplif := "dead_fallen"]

# Invalid trees (for many reasons)
status_info[.(c(6, 7, 8)), status_simplif := "invalid"]

# Lost trees (without any trace, no stump nada wallou)
status_info[.(9), status_simplif := "not_found"]

# Not sampled trees
status_info[.(c(10, 11, 1111)), status_simplif := "not_sampled"]

# Failed trees
status_info[.(c(2002, 2007, 2008, 2012, 2017, 2022)), status_simplif := "failed"]

#### Specification for dead trees
dead_tab = unlist(ls_paths_lookup[["/lookup_dead_wood_type"]][["get"]][["tags"]])

dead_info = request(endpoint) |>
	req_url_path_append(dead_tab) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "lookup"
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE) |>
	setDT()

#### Specification for stem form and breakage
## Form
current_tab = unlist(ls_paths_lookup[["/lookup_stem_breakage"]][["get"]][["tags"]])

break_info = request(endpoint) |>
	req_url_path_append(current_tab) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "lookup"
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE) |>
	setDT()

break_info = break_info[, .(code, name_en)] |>
	setkey(code)

# Simplify the breakage definitions
break_info[.(0), break_simplif := "not_broken"]
break_info[.(1), break_simplif := "broken_top"]
break_info[.(2), break_simplif := "broken_crown"]

## Breakage
current_tab = unlist(ls_paths_lookup[["/lookup_stem_form"]][["get"]][["tags"]])

form_info = request(endpoint) |>
	req_url_path_append(current_tab) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "lookup"
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE) |>

form_info = form_info[, .(code, name_en)] |>

# Simplify the form definitions
form_info[.(0), form_simplif := "forked_crown"]
form_info[.(1), form_simplif := "straight"]
form_info[.(2), form_simplif := "forked"]
form_info[.(3), form_simplif := "twin"]
form_info[.(c(4, 5, 6)), form_simplif := "dead_1987"]
```

### Query tree data

The data can be found in the `inventory_archive` schema, which contains the following tables:

- inventory_archive
	- cluster
	- plot
	- edges
	- deadwood
	- regeneration
	- structure_lt4m
	- structure_gt4m
	- subplot_position
	- tree

This is a more complex query, and help can be found on [Thünen institute's github](https://thuenen-forest-ecosystems.github.io/TFM-Documentation/api/inventory_loop.html) in order to combine API calls to get larger amounts of data.

#### Step 1: Retrieve list of cluster names

This time, I do it on the `inventory_archive` schema. I first extract all the paths and keep the interesting ones.

```{r}
#### List tables in data base
## Get all clusters
table_ls = request(endpoint) |>
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "inventory_archive" 
	) |>
	req_perform() |>
	resp_body_json()

names(table_ls)

ls_paths_inventory = table_ls[["paths"]]
sort(names(ls_paths_inventory))

table_dt = data.table(path = names(ls_paths_inventory), extract = FALSE, key = "path")
table_dt[c("/tree", "/plot", "/cluster"), extract := TRUE]

## Subset to interesting clusters
table_dt = table_dt[(extract)]
```

Then, I get the number of rows for each table.
```{r}
#### Get dimensions
n_rows = data.table(path = table_dt[, path], n = NA_integer_, key = "path")

for (current_path in table_dt[, path])
{
	temp = request(endpoint) |>
	req_url_path_append(current_path) |>
	req_url_query(limit = 0) |> # Avoid downloading any data
	req_headers(
		apikey = apikey,
		Accept = "application/json",
		`Accept-Profile` = "inventory_archive",
		Prefer = "count=exact"
	) |>
	req_perform()

	str = resp_header(temp, "content-range")
	lim = stri_sub(str, from = stri_locate_first(str, regex = "/")[, "end"] + 1)
	n_rows[current_path, n := as.integer(lim)]
}
```

#### Step 2: Run extraction for the clusters of interest

Now, I query data with the provided paths. Note that the tables `tree_coordinates` and `plot_coordinates` were returned empty. I suspect that it contains real coordinates, and that a special key is needed to access these tables. This is why I chose `tree` and `plot`.

```{r}
if (!file.exists("../data/request_germany.rds"))
{
	full_req = vector(mode = "list", length = table_dt[, .N])
	names(full_req) = table_dt[, path]

	page_size = 15000 # API limit is 2e4 (tried the 3rd November 2026)

	for (current_path in table_dt[, path])
	{
		lim = n_rows[current_path, n]
		n_pages = ceiling(lim/page_size) 
		offset = 0

		p_counter = 1

		full_req[[current_path]] = vector(mode = "list", length = n_pages)

		while (p_counter <= n_pages)
		{
			full_req[[current_path]][[p_counter]] = request(endpoint) |>
				req_url_path_append(current_path) |>
				req_url_query(
					limit = page_size,
					offset = offset
				) |>
				req_headers(
					apikey = apikey,
					Accept = "application/json",
					`Accept-Profile` = "inventory_archive"
				) |>
				req_throttle(capacity = 30, fill_time_s = 60, realm = current_path) |> # 30 request per minute max
				req_perform() |>
				resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE) |>
				setDT()

			print(paste0(round(p_counter/n_pages * 100, 2), "% done for <", current_path, ">"))
			
			offset = p_counter*page_size
			p_counter = p_counter + 1
		}

		full_req[[current_path]] = rbindlist(l = full_req[[current_path]], fill = TRUE, idcol = "page")
	}

	saveRDS(full_req, "../data/request_germany.rds")
} else {
	full_req = readRDS("../data/request_germany.rds")
}
```

#### Step 3: Format the extracted data and merge

For the `cluster` table, I want to keep the following fields:

- id: The id of the cluster!
- inspire_grid_cell

For the `plot` table, I want to keep the following fields:

- cluster_id
- plot_name
- id: The id of the plot, NOT cluster! However, there are different ids for a single `plot_name`! I think the `id` changes with the cycle, and is a unique identifier, while `plot_name` is carrying through cycles.
- interval_name
- acquisition_date
- management_type
- stand_age
- stand_structure
- terrain_slope

For the `tree` table, I want to keep the following fields:

- plot_id
- tree_number
- tree_status
- tree_species
- dbh
- dbh_height
- tree_height
- stem_height
- tree_age
- stem_breakage
- stem_form

```{r}
cols = c("id", "inspire_grid_cell", "is_training")
cluster_dt = full_req[["/cluster"]][, ..cols] |>
	setnames(old = "id", new = "cluster_id")

check_na = cluster_dt[is.na(inspire_grid_cell), all(is_training)] &&
	cluster_dt[!is.na(inspire_grid_cell), !any(is_training)]

if (check_na)
{
	print("NAs in cluster_dt are only for the clusters that were used for training")
} else {
	warning("I thought that NAs in cluster_dt were only used for 'training' type, but it is not the case")
}

cols = c("cluster_id", "plot_name", "id", "interval_name", "acquisition_date", "management_type",
	"stand_age", "stand_structure", "terrain_slope")
plot_dt = full_req[["/plot"]][, ..cols] |>
	setnames(old = "id", new = "plot_id") |>
	merge.data.table(y = cluster_dt, by = "cluster_id")

cols = c("plot_id", "tree_number", "tree_species", "tree_status", "dbh", "dbh_height", "tree_height",
	"stem_height", "tree_age", "stem_breakage", "stem_form", "damage_dead", "deadwood_used")
tree_dt = full_req[["/tree"]][, ..cols] |>
	merge.data.table(plot_dt, by = "plot_id")
```

### Get coordinates

According to Sebastian Schnell (Thübingen institute) who promptly replied to my e-mail (hahaha hilarious!!!), the offset coordinates are linked to the 1 km INSPIRE grid via the column `inspire_grid_cell` in the cluster table. They do not provide the grid itself but it can be downloaded on the [Bundesamt für Kartographie und Geodäsie's website](https://gdz.bkg.bund.de/index.php/default/inspire/sonstige-inspire-themen/geographische-gitter-fur-deutschland-in-lambert-projektion-geogitter-inspire.html).

Therefore, I only need to use the column `inspire_grid_cell` from `tree_dt` and then extract the coordinates from the geopackage file, using the `id`, which as the exact same format as `inspire_grid_cell`, such as 1kmN579E47. Then, I choose to associate the middle coordinate of the grid cell, `(x_mp, y_mp)` to the clusters, and therefore the plots.

```{r}
#### Add coordinates to tree_dt
## Load Deutschland 1km resolution, EPSG 3035 from Bundesamt für Kartographie und Geodäsie
deutschland = vect("../data/DE_Grid_ETRS89-LAEA_1km.gpkg/geogitter/DE_Grid_ETRS89-LAEA_1km.gpkg")
info = as.data.table(crs(deutschland, describe = TRUE))
info[, .(authority, code)]

coords = as.data.table(deutschland)[, .(id, x_mp, y_mp)] |>
	setnames(old = c("x_mp", "y_mp"), new = c("x_epsg_3035", "y_epsg_3035")) 

## Merge
tree_dt = merge.data.table(tree_dt, coords, by.x = "inspire_grid_cell", by.y = "id", all.x = TRUE)

## Check missing data
check_na = tree_dt[is.na(x_epsg_3035), all(is_training)] &&
	tree_dt[!is.na(x_epsg_3035), !any(is_training)]

if (check_na)
{
	print("All the NAs coordinates are for the training plots")
} else {
	warning("I thought that NAs were only for 'training' plots, but it is not the case")
}

## Remove missing coordinates
tree_dt = tree_dt[!(is_training)]
```

### Add information

Columns that have codes, such as `tree_species`, are explained in the `lookup` schema. I already gathered the necessary data in @sec-lookup and only need to merge them in what follows.

#### Tree status

The column `tree_status` contains codes that describe the status of the tree. The codes 0 and 1 potentially contains dead trees! I expect NAs in dbh when the tree is dead. All the other codes will be discarded later.

```{r}
tree_dt = merge.data.table(tree_dt, status_info[, .(code, status_simplif)],
	by.x = "tree_status", by.y = "code", all.x = TRUE)
```

#### Species name

```{r}
#### Add species
## Merge genus and species
species_dt[, speciesName_sci := paste(genus, species)] |>
	setkey(speciesName_sci)

## Merge data tables
tree_dt = merge.data.table(tree_dt, species_dt[, .(nfi_code, speciesName_sci, genus)],
	by.x = "tree_species", by.y = "nfi_code", all.x = TRUE)

## Check NAs
check_na = "sampled" %notin% tree_dt[is.na(speciesName_sci), unique(status_simplif)]

if (check_na)
{
	print("All the sampled trees have a species specified")
	tree_dt = tree_dt[!is.na(speciesName_sci)]
} else {
	warning("Not all sampled trees have a specified species. Check these NAs!!")
}
```

#### Breakage and form

```{r}
#### Add breakage and form information
tree_dt = merge.data.table(tree_dt, form_info[, .(code, form_simplif)],
	by.x = "stem_form", by.y = "code", all.x = TRUE)

tree_dt = merge.data.table(tree_dt, break_info[, .(code, break_simplif)],
	by.x = "stem_breakage", by.y = "code", all.x = TRUE)

## Remove the forms that are 4, 5, or 6 as these are dead trees (1987 inventory west Germany)
tree_dt = tree_dt[stem_form %notin% c(4, 5, 6)]

## Check NAs in breakage
check_na = ("sampled" %notin% tree_dt[is.na(break_simplif), table(status_simplif)]) &&
	(tree_dt[is.na(break_simplif), .N] != 0)

if (check_na | tree_dt[is.na(break_simplif), .N] == 0)
{
	print("None of the trees with missing break information were sampled")
	tree_dt = tree_dt[!is.na(break_simplif)]
} else {
	warning("Some sampled trees have missing breakage information. Check these NAs!!")
}
```

### Check diameters at breast height NAs

There are `NAs` in the dbh. I found that sampled trees all have a dbh

```{r}
#### Check NAs...
## ...in dbh
check_na = ("sampled" %notin% tree_dt[is.na(dbh), unique(status_simplif)]) &&
	(tree_dt[is.na(dbh), .N] != 0)

if (check_na | tree_dt[is.na(dbh), .N] == 0)
{
	print("All the sampled trees have a dbh measured")
	tree_dt = tree_dt[!is.na(dbh)]
} else {
	warning("Not all sampled trees have a measured dbh. Check these NAs!!")
}

## ..in acquisition date
tree_dt = tree_dt[!is.na(acquisition_date)]
```

### Prepare coordinates for Jonathan

Following Jonathan's advice, I focus on two species, *Fagus sylvatica* and *Picea abies*. I subset `tree_dt` to these to species and decided to keep:

1. Non-broken trees only and not 'damaged dead'
2. Only straight and crown-forked trees. I remove twins and forked, as they probably have different growing responses, and NAs for uncertainty
3. Trees measured at least twice (after filtering for everyhting else!)
4. Tree with diameter measured at breast height (130 cm)
5. Trees that are consistent in terms of species

```{r}
# lala = copy(tree_dt)
# tree_dt = copy(lala)

#### Subsetting...
## ...at the breast height level (only keep 1.3 m)
tree_dt = tree_dt[dbh_height == 130]

## ... at the species level (1 species per id, subset to Fag syl and Pic abi)
tree_dt[, unique_id := paste(cluster_id, plot_name, tree_number, sep = "_")]
tree_dt[, check_sp := length(unique(speciesName_sci)), by = unique_id]
tree_dt = tree_dt[check_sp == 1]
tree_dt[, check_sp := NULL]

tree_dt = tree_dt[speciesName_sci %in% c("Fagus sylvatica", "Picea abies")]

## ...at the tree form level
tree_dt[, .N, by = .(speciesName_sci, form_simplif)]
tree_dt = tree_dt[form_simplif %in% c("straight", "forked_crown")]

## ...at the health level
tree_dt[, .N, by = .(speciesName_sci, break_simplif)]
tree_dt = tree_dt[break_simplif %in% c("not_broken")]

tree_dt = tree_dt[!(damage_dead)]

## ... at the measurement level
tree_dt[, n_measure := .N, by = .(cluster_id, plot_name, tree_number)]

tree_dt = tree_dt[n_measure > 1]
tree_dt[, n_measure := NULL]

# zozo = copy(tree_dt)
# tree_dt = copy(zozo)
```

### Save the tree data

Before saving, I compute growth and check if growth is positive? Given that trees are meaured every ten years, it is unlikely to get negative growth due to small tape error and size variation due to water content in the trunk. Therefore, negative growth will likely come from extreme error or extreme events (hole in the trunk, peeled bark, other stuff?). Given that I filtered to 'healthy trees', I think negative growth can therefore only come from 'extreme errors' (i.e., typo), and not from the 'routine error' (tape variation in position and extension).

```{r}
#### Check-up negative growth
## Compute growth
# Order trees by unique id and date for computation
setkey(tree_dt, unique_id, acquisition_date)

# Remove some columns, sort out. stem_height is almost NA 92% of the time...
rm_cols = c("stem_breakage", "stem_form", "tree_species", "tree_status",
	"inspire_grid_cell", "plot_id", "dbh_height", "damage_dead",
	"deadwood_used", "is_training", "status_simplif", "stem_height")

tree_dt[, (rm_cols) := NULL] |> setcolorder()

coords_jonathan = vect(unique(tree_dt[, .(x_epsg_3035, y_epsg_3035)]),
	geom = c("x_epsg_3035", "y_epsg_3035"),
	crs = paste(info[, authority], info[, code], sep = ":"))

filename = "../data/coords_jonathan-deutschland.gpkg"
if (!file.exists(filename))
{
	writeVector(coords_jonathan, filename, overwrite = TRUE, options = "ENCODING=UTF-8")
} else{
	coords_jonathan = vect(filename)
}
```
